I hid it. Even my parents and many of my closest friends had no idea I would pour hours and hours into my stories weekly, or even daily. This year, though, I took a high school writing class, which accompanied my English class. My teacher not only writes but is also very well-respected in the theater community, and has written several original pieces. It was only recently that I had the opportunity to write something creative for his class--a script for an original scene--and by the time I got around to it, I was exhausted from all of my academic work. I wrote the script in under two hours. It was far from my best work, but I simply didn't have the extra time to put into it. After I turned it in, my writing teacher approached me and told me it was outstanding, that he wished he'd had the opportunity to read my creative writing earlier, and that he wanted me to polish it and enter it in a short play contest next year. I'd hidden my love of writing for three years, and almost nobody had ever read, let alone praised, my work, so I was blown away--and I still am. I never dreamed that my "hobby" could be worth acknowledging, but now I was finally being told it was--not by the school system, but by a man who worked in a creative field. In the past few weeks I've opened up more and let more and more people read my work, again, outside of the school curriculum, and I've been told time and time again that I have a promising future in creative writing, if I choose to take it. I've been offered advice, I've been called a prodigy, people have offered to mentor me--it's astounding. And nothing I've shown people has been my best work! But I still have a hard time wrapping my mind around the idea that my creative achievements are more important than my academic ones...because only academic achievement is praised by the school system. I still have to sacrifice most of my time to math and science, because in the eyes of the school system, my writing is not worth a grade. In the eyes of the school system, my passion, my devotion to a creative outlet, means nothing.
I'm not the only person I know in this situation--my experience might be somewhat of an extreme case, but I know gifted artists and musicians who are also seeing their talent and creativity squandered by the school system. I've seen it at every school I've ever been to, with dozens and dozens of passionate people. I've witnessed the exact moment when people gave up on their dreams because they were told math and science were more important than what they loved. The school system kills creativity.

One of the biggest things I took out of it was
that I felt like he was trying to get across the point that everyone is
creative, but you’re not allowed to be creative in academics. He made the point
that schools prepare children to be college professors RATHER than to help them
be creative, as though a professor must be exempt from being able to have
original ideas. He also made the joke that during a social interaction,
academics are praying for it to end so that they can “go write a paper about it,”
as if to devalue talking about things in a structured way as a viable outlet of
expression. All throughout school, I was one of the few kids that valued
academics above everything else. When somebody asked me, “what’s your hobby?”
and I responded “doing math or learning about physics” people would respond,
“but what do you like to do for fun?” I’d have to give the answer “I play the
piano” instead because it’s a more acceptable answer as a leisure activity. But
I could do math the way a “normal” person my age played sports or played video
games. I could sit down and solve problem after problem for hours, or rearrange
problems and make my own in order to give myself a better understanding of a
mathematical concept. And then I could apply that concept to a physical
situation to find links between things in the real world that I never would
have realized otherwise. I don’t consider myself good at either math or
physics. Were I to ever achieve great success in the fields I would not want my
achievements to precede me the same way high achievers in the arts often seem
to. I would not want my achievements to precede me because I believe that I am
not good at the topics, I merely enjoy them, and I wouldn’t want someone to
feel like I was better than them just because I enjoyed something they didn’t.
Most, if not all people can do math faster than me. I am extremely slow at
doing my work, and for most of my life I felt like that was supposed to mean
that I wasn’t good at it. Eventually, I even grew to hate mathematics. However, at the height of my loathing in the 10th grade, I discovered that if
I tried hard enough, I could comprehend graduate level texts. I was impressed
with myself for this, and unlike the other things in life that I had wanted to
be good at in order to impress others (which admittedly is why I started doing
more complicated mathematics at first), I could do something that I myself
could be proud of, and I realized that was all that mattered. I derived great
joy from discovering new ideas and the ways they link together, or finding my
own new ways to understand something. I have even been brought to tears by the
beauty I find in mathematics, as silly as that may sound. I would even argue,
physics and mathematics are fields that praise creative individuals, as some of
the most notable physicists in history include the likes of Albert Einstein and
Richard Feynman, two men who revolutionized physics by working on ideas that
everyone had worked on before, but in entirely new ways. So, I'd that no, he is wrong. Schools could certainly be reworked to be more inclusive of children that like to do things like dance, sing, paint, etc., or just be more accepting of students that enjoy different
things and learn in different ways in general, but for some, the academic areas
in school are the places THEY get to show off their creativity, and in a world
that continues to attempt to be more inclusive of those we think are being
ignored, we must refrain ourselves from putting the kids we commonly see as
“uncreative” or “creative in the wrong ways” on the back burner, in favor of
those that we think are being ignored.

Do schools kill creativity? | Sir Ken Robinson 
 Throughout the speech, Sir Ken Robinson mainly discusses that schools suppress children's creativity. Schools today tend to treat mistakes as an unforgivable fault, as we can see teachers who go furious when we choose the wrong answer by mistake. Mistakes don't precisely signify creativity, but most revolutionary advances have derived from creative ideas thought to be a 'mistake' in that society. As schools make children fear making mistakes, they grow up to lose the ability to create something inventive and ingenious. Moreover, this phenomenon is occurring throughout the whole world. Schools kill children's creativity not only by prohibiting mistakes but by underestimating subjects regarding creativity so as art and dance. The speaker claims that this phenomenon occurs throughout the whole world since most countries consider the ultimate goal of public education is training professors, which requires not creativity but logic. Likewise, creativity is underrated since it is not essential in industrialized society. What jobs require defines people's value. Artists and musicians make less money, so they are less needed. Following society's common demand of intelligence, university naturally changed into the job training center. The presenter strongly argues that this view on education should be viewed differently. For example, ADHD is defined as an attention disorder, yet if we change our attitude toward it, we can find that people with ADHD are talented in bodily activities such as dancing. In conclusion, the author asserts that humans' future depends on whether they adjust their new concept of the education system which can lead to the flourishing of humanity.
 Even if the presentation was taken more than ten years ago, his idea is determined to be true. Also, the problem he mentioned is still not settled in Korea. What estimates people's value is the university and the specialty they majored in. Korea has not adapted to the fourth industrial revolution, concerned with computing technology that needs creativity. Exams in schools are taken not to give students motivation to study but to exclude them from success. Students in Korea are not "studying" but "memorizing" technical terms that they never understand. How could they make software and A.I.s though they have never created something new throughout their whole life? It is essential to reconsider the nature of the study.

Mathematics is one of the most fundamental and universal disciplines in human knowledge. It is often described as the language of the universe because it provides a precise way to describe patterns, structures, relationships, and changes. From the simplest act of counting objects to the most complex theories about space and time, math plays a central role in understanding both the natural world and human-made systems.

At its core, mathematics is about patterns and logic. Early humans likely developed basic mathematical ideas out of necessity—counting food, measuring land, or tracking time. Over centuries, these simple beginnings evolved into a vast and sophisticated field. Today, mathematics includes many branches such as arithmetic, algebra, geometry, calculus, statistics, and more, each dealing with different kinds of problems and methods.

Arithmetic is the most basic branch and deals with numbers and operations like addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division. It is the foundation upon which all other mathematical concepts are built. Without arithmetic, everyday tasks such as shopping, budgeting, or telling time would be extremely difficult.

Algebra extends arithmetic by introducing symbols, usually letters, to represent numbers. This allows for the formulation of general rules and the solving of equations. Instead of working with specific numbers, algebra enables us to describe relationships and patterns abstractly. For example, rather than saying “3 + 5 = 8,” algebra allows us to write “a + b = c,” which can represent countless specific situations.

Geometry focuses on shapes, sizes, and the properties of space. It examines objects such as points, lines, angles, and surfaces. Geometry is not only theoretical but also highly practical. It is essential in fields like architecture, engineering, and art. The design of buildings, bridges, and even digital graphics relies heavily on geometric principles.

Calculus, one of the more advanced branches of mathematics, deals with change and motion. It is divided into differential calculus, which studies rates of change, and integral calculus, which deals with accumulation and areas. Calculus is crucial in physics, engineering, economics, and many other disciplines. It allows scientists to model how things move, grow, or change over time, such as predicting the trajectory of a rocket or understanding population growth.

Statistics and probability deal with data, uncertainty, and decision-making. In a world filled with information, these branches are more important than ever. Statistics helps us collect, analyze, and interpret data, while probability measures the likelihood of events. Together, they are used in fields like medicine, business, politics, and social sciences to make informed decisions and predictions.

One of the unique features of mathematics is its reliance on logical reasoning and proof. Unlike many other subjects, math does not depend on opinions or beliefs. A mathematical statement is considered true only if it can be proven using a clear and logical argument. This emphasis on proof ensures that mathematical knowledge is reliable and consistent.

Mathematics is also highly interconnected. Concepts from one area often apply to others, creating a rich web of relationships. For example, algebra is used in geometry to describe shapes, while calculus relies on algebraic and geometric ideas. This interconnectedness allows mathematicians to approach problems from multiple perspectives and develop deeper insights.

In addition to its practical uses, mathematics has a strong element of beauty and creativity. Many mathematicians describe their work as an art form. Elegant solutions, symmetrical patterns, and surprising connections can evoke a sense of wonder. For instance, simple equations can generate intricate fractals, and basic numerical sequences can appear in nature, such as in the arrangement of leaves or the spirals of shells.

Mathematics is also essential in modern technology. Computers, smartphones, and the internet all rely on mathematical principles. Algorithms, which are step-by-step procedures for solving problems, are at the heart of computer science. Cryptography, the practice of secure communication, uses complex mathematical techniques to protect data. Even artificial intelligence and machine learning are built upon mathematical foundations, particularly in linear algebra, probability, and optimization.

Despite its importance, many people find mathematics challenging or intimidating. This often stems from the way it is taught or perceived. Math is sometimes presented as a set of rigid rules to memorize rather than a dynamic and meaningful discipline. However, when approached with curiosity and patience, math can become an engaging and rewarding subject. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, and logical reasoning—skills that are valuable in all areas of life.

This video is a fun overview of math, but it contains several simplifications and a few actual mistakes. Some parts are correct, like the explanations of variables, constants, inverse operations, the Pythagorean theorem, SOH-CAH-TOA trig ratios, the idea of functions mapping inputs to outputs, derivatives representing rates of change, integrals representing accumulated area, and basic probability rules like probabilities being between 0 and 1 and summing to 1. However, several statements are misleading or incorrect. We do not actually know whether the universe is infinite. Saying the goal of every equation is to be solved is oversimplified since many equations are studied for behavior rather than explicit solutions. Saying variables in quadratic or polynomial equations “equal multiple values at the same time” is poorly phrased because the equation simply has multiple possible solutions. The claim that every shape uses area = base × height is false since many shapes like triangles, circles, and trapezoids use different formulas. The statement that turning points depend on how many variables a function has is incorrect because they depend on the degree of the polynomial. Saying a function becomes discontinuous if it equals zero is also wrong since many continuous functions equal zero at some points. The explanations of limits, derivatives, integrals, and the unit circle are mostly right but simplified for beginners. Overall the video is entertaining and mostly fine as a quick conceptual introduction, but it should not be treated as a precise or rigorous explanation of mathematics.
